Appendix

D

Glossary

Every key term from the 25 chapters, in alphabetical order, with the chapter that explains it. A term defined in more than one chapter has one line per chapter.

A

ABAC
Attribute-based access control: rules over attributes of principal, resource, action and context. (Chapter 6)
Access control matrix
Principals × resources, with permitted actions in each cell. (Chapter 6)
Access entry
An EKS mapping from an IAM principal to Kubernetes permissions. (Chapter 16)
Access inventory
A list of every kind of principal, how it authenticates, what it can reach and who owns it. (Chapter 25)
Access review
A periodic confirmation of who has access, by someone who knows. (Chapter 13)
Access token
A short-lived token sent to APIs. (Chapter 3)
Account assignment
A user or group, a permission set and an account. (Chapter 12)
Account ID
The 12-digit number identifying an account, part of every ARN. (Chapter 7)
Accountability
Recording who did what, when, so actions can be traced to identities. (Chapter 1)
ACL
Access control list: the permissions stored on one resource. (Chapter 6)
ACS URL
Assertion consumer service: the SP endpoint that receives SAML responses. (Chapter 5)
Action
One API operation, written service:Operation. (Chapter 9)
Alternate contacts
Billing, operations and security contacts AWS uses for notices. (Chapter 7)
ARN
Amazon Resource Name: the unique identifier of an AWS resource. (Chapter 9)
Assertion
A signed SAML statement about a subject's authentication and attributes. (Chapter 5)
AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
The STS call that exchanges an OIDC token for role credentials. (Chapter 17)
Attributes for access control
Identity attributes passed into sessions as tags, for ABAC. (Chapter 12)
Audience
The service a token is meant for; others must reject it. (Chapter 3)
Authentication
Proving a claimed identity with a credential. (Chapter 1)
Authorisation
Deciding whether an authenticated principal may perform an action on a resource. (Chapter 1)
Authoriser
The component that authenticates callers in front of an API. (Chapter 19)
Authorization code
A short-lived, one-time reference exchanged for tokens on the back channel. (Chapter 4)
Authorization server
Authenticates the user, collects consent and issues tokens. (Chapter 4)
AWS access portal
The page where people sign in and choose an account and permission set. (Chapter 12)
AWS account
A container for resources, identities and billing, isolated from other accounts. (Chapter 7)
AWS Organization
A group of accounts under central management, billing and policy. (Chapter 20)
AWS RAM
Resource Access Manager: shares resources across accounts and OUs. (Chapter 21)
aws:PrincipalArn
The ARN of the calling user or role (a role session's role), used for exceptions. (Chapter 10)
aws:PrincipalOrgID
The organisation of the calling principal. (Chapter 22)
aws:ResourceOrgID
The organisation that owns the resource being accessed. (Chapter 22)
aws:SourceArn / aws:SourceAccount
Condition keys naming the resource or account a service acts for. (Chapter 21)
aws:SourceOrgID
The organisation of the resource an AWS service is acting for. (Chapter 22)
aws:SourceVpc / aws:SourceVpce
The VPC or VPC endpoint a request came through. (Chapter 22)
aws:ViaAWSService
True when an AWS service makes a request on a principal's behalf. (Chapter 22)

B

Bearer token
A token that grants access to whoever presents it. (Chapter 3)
Birthright access
Access granted automatically from attributes such as department. (Chapter 13)
Break-glass access
Emergency access that works when normal sign-in doesn't. (Chapter 14)

C

Canonical request
The normalised form of a request that gets hashed and signed. (Chapter 19)
Centralised root access
Removing member accounts' root credentials and doing root tasks through scoped sessions. (Chapter 7)
check-access-not-granted
An Access Analyzer check that a policy doesn't allow listed actions or resources. (Chapter 24)
check-no-new-access
An Access Analyzer check that a new policy version grants nothing the old one didn't. (Chapter 24)
Claim
A statement in a token, such as sub, aud or exp. (Chapter 3)
Client
The application requesting access; confidential (can keep a secret) or public. (Chapter 4)
CloudTrail
AWS's record of API calls in an account. (Chapter 11)
Code owners
People or teams whose approval a repository requires for changes to given paths. (Chapter 24)
Condition key
A value AWS knows about a request, compared in a condition block. (Chapter 9)
Confused deputy
A privileged service tricked into acting for someone without that privilege. (Chapter 21)
Credential
What a principal shows to authenticate: a password, key, token or certificate. (Chapter 1)
Credential provider chain
The order in which tools look for credentials. (Chapter 8)
Credential report
A CSV of every IAM user and root, with password, MFA and access key status. (Chapter 7)
Credential scope
Date, region and service that a SigV4 signature is valid for. (Chapter 19)
Credential stuffing
Logging in with username–password pairs leaked from other sites. (Chapter 2)
Cross-account role
A role whose trust policy names a principal in another account. (Chapter 21)

D

Data event
A data-plane call such as S3 object access; recorded only if a trail asks for it. (Chapter 11)
Data key
A key generated per object or batch to encrypt data locally. (Chapter 18)
Data perimeter
Preventive guardrails ensuring only trusted identities reach trusted resources from expected networks. (Chapter 22)
Default deny
The rule that anything not explicitly allowed is denied. (Chapter 1)
Delegated administrator
A member account allowed to run an organisation-wide service. (Chapter 20)
Deploy-time least privilege
Giving a pipeline only the permissions a deployment needs. (Chapter 17)
Deprovisioning
Deactivating or deleting a person's accounts and access. (Chapter 13)
Discovery
The /.well-known/openid-configuration document describing a provider. (Chapter 4)
Drift
A difference between what the code says and what exists. (Chapter 24)

E

EKS Pod Identity / IRSA
Two ways to give a service account its own IAM role. (Chapter 16)
Elevation
Activating eligible privilege, with justification and often approval. (Chapter 14)
Eligibility
Being allowed to request a privilege, without holding it. (Chapter 14)
Encoded authorization message
A denial's details in encoded form, decoded with sts:DecodeAuthorizationMessage. (Chapter 11)
Encryption context
Key–value pairs bound to an encryption, required to decrypt and logged. (Chapter 18)
Envelope encryption
Encrypting data with a data key and the data key with a KMS key. (Chapter 18)
Explicit deny
A matching Deny statement in any policy; always wins. (Chapter 10)
External ID
A vendor-generated, per-customer value required in a trust policy. (Chapter 21)

F

Federation
Accepting another system's authentication of a person. (Chapter 5)
FullAWSAccess
The default SCP that allows everything through a level. (Chapter 20)

G

Grant
A temporary, narrow permission on a KMS key, usually created by a service. (Chapter 18)
GuardDuty
AWS's managed threat detection service. (Chapter 23)
Guardrail
A deny that holds regardless of other permissions. (Chapter 10)

H

Home realm discovery
Working out which IdP a person belongs to. (Chapter 5)
Hop limit
How many network hops IMDSv2's token response may travel. (Chapter 15)

I

IAM Access Analyzer
The AWS tool that validates policies and generates them from activity. (Chapter 9)
Finds external and unused access, and checks policies. (Chapter 23)
IAM group
A set of IAM users sharing policies; not a principal. (Chapter 8)
IAM Identity Center
AWS's workforce sign-in service for accounts and applications. (Chapter 12)
IAM OIDC identity provider
The IAM resource that tells AWS to trust an issuer's tokens. (Chapter 17)
IAM role
An identity without credentials, assumed for temporary sessions. (Chapter 8)
IAM Roles Anywhere
Role sessions for workloads outside AWS, authenticated with X.509 certificates. (Chapter 15)
IAM user
A long-lived identity with a password and/or access keys in one account. (Chapter 8)
iam:PassRole
The permission to give a role to an AWS service. (Chapter 8)
ID token
An OIDC JWT, addressed to the client, describing the authentication. (Chapter 4)
Identification
Claiming an identity, such as a user name. (Chapter 1)
Identity as code
Managing roles, policies and assignments as reviewed files that a pipeline applies. (Chapter 24)
Identity provider (IdP)
A system that authenticates principals and issues tokens describing them. (Chapter 1)
Authenticates people and issues signed assertions about them. (Chapter 5)
Identity source
Where Identity Center's users and groups come from. (Chapter 12)
Identity-based policy
A policy attached to a user, group or role. (Chapter 9)
IMDSv2
The session-oriented metadata service: PUT for a token, then token on each request. (Chapter 15)
Implicit deny
The default result when nothing allows a request. (Chapter 10)
Instance metadata service
The link-local endpoint that serves an instance's details and role credentials. (Chapter 15)
Instance profile
The container that attaches a role to an EC2 instance. (Chapter 15)
invokedBy
The service that made a call on a principal's behalf. (Chapter 11)

J

JIT provisioning
Creating an account at a person's first federated sign-in. (Chapter 5)
Joiner, mover, leaver
The three lifecycle events that change a person's access. (Chapter 13)
Just-in-time access
Privilege activated for a limited time when needed. (Chapter 14)
JWKS
JSON Web Key Set: an issuer's published public keys. (Chapter 3)
JWT
JSON Web Token: base64url-encoded header and claims, plus a signature. (Chapter 3)

K

Key policy
The resource-based policy that controls a KMS key. (Chapter 18)
KMS key
A key held in AWS KMS's hardware, used to wrap data keys or encrypt small data. (Chapter 18)
Kubernetes RBAC
Kubernetes' allow-only, role-based authorisation for its API. (Chapter 16)

L

Last accessed information
Which services and actions an identity has actually used, and when. (Chapter 11)
Least privilege
Only the access needed, for only as long as needed. (Chapter 6)

M

Managed / inline policy
A standalone, reusable policy, versus one embedded in a single identity. (Chapter 9)
Management account
The account that creates and pays for an AWS Organization. (Chapter 7)
The account that owns the organisation; not restricted by SCPs or RCPs. (Chapter 20)
Management event
A control-plane call (create, change, delete, many reads); recorded by default. (Chapter 11)
Metadata
An XML description of an IdP or SP: entity ID, endpoints and certificates. (Chapter 5)
MFA
Multi-factor authentication: two or more different kinds of factor. (Chapter 2)
Mutual TLS
TLS where the client also presents a certificate. (Chapter 19)

N

NameID
The identifier for the subject; persistent NameIDs never change for a person and SP. (Chapter 5)
Node role
The IAM role of an EKS worker node. (Chapter 16)

O

OAuth 2.0
A framework for granting applications limited access to resources on a user's behalf. (Chapter 4)
OIDC federation
Trusting tokens from an external OpenID Connect issuer to grant role sessions. (Chapter 17)
OpenID Connect
An identity layer on OAuth 2.0 that adds sign-in and ID tokens. (Chapter 4)
Organisation instance
An Identity Center instance in an organisation, able to grant AWS account access. (Chapter 12)
Organisation trail
A CloudTrail trail recording every account in an organisation. (Chapter 23)
Organisational unit (OU)
A container of accounts to which policies attach. (Chapter 20)
Origin
The scheme, host and port of a web page, such as https://larder.example. (Chapter 2)

P

Passkey
A FIDO2/WebAuthn credential: a per-site key pair whose private key stays on the user's device or keychain. (Chapter 2)
Password hashing function
A deliberately slow, often memory-hard hash such as Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt. (Chapter 2)
PEP / PDP
Policy enforcement point (blocks the request) and policy decision point (decides). (Chapter 1)
Permission set
A template of policies and session length that becomes a role in each assigned account. (Chapter 12)
Permissions boundary
A managed policy that caps an identity's maximum permissions. (Chapter 10)
Phishing-resistant
An authenticator whose output can't be relayed to a site other than the one it was made for. (Chapter 2)
Pilot light
A minimal copy of critical systems in another region, ready to be scaled up in a disaster. (Chapter 25)
PKCE
Proof Key for Code Exchange: a secret verifier that proves the redeemer of a code started the flow. (Chapter 4)
Policy
A JSON document of statements that allow or deny actions on resources. (Chapter 9)
Policy engine
A component that evaluates authorisation rules and returns allow or deny. (Chapter 6)
Policy generation
Drafting a policy from a role's recorded activity in CloudTrail. (Chapter 24)
Policy simulator
AWS's tool for evaluating a principal's policies against chosen requests. (Chapter 11)
Policy variable
A ${…} placeholder filled in from the request at evaluation time. (Chapter 9)
Principal
A person or workload that can make requests and be granted access. (Chapter 1)
Principal tag / resource tag
Key-value pairs on an identity or a resource, used for ABAC. (Chapter 9)
Privilege creep
Access accumulating over time as people move and cover. (Chapter 6)
Privileged access
Permissions that can cause serious harm or grant more access. (Chapter 14)
Projected token
A short-lived, audience-bound service account JWT mounted into a pod. (Chapter 16)
Protected environment
A GitHub environment with deployment rules such as required reviewers. (Chapter 17)
Provisioning
Creating, updating and removing accounts and group memberships in apps. (Chapter 13)

R

RBAC
Role-based access control: permissions granted to roles, roles assigned to principals. (Chapter 6)
RCP
Resource control policy: an organisation ceiling on access to resources in member accounts. (Chapter 10)
Resource control policy: a ceiling on access to resources in member accounts. (Chapter 20)
ReBAC
Relationship-based access control: decisions follow relationships between objects. (Chapter 6)
Refresh token
A longer-lived, revocable token used only to get new access tokens. (Chapter 3)
Replay
Re-sending a captured, valid request. (Chapter 19)
Resource-based policy
A policy attached to a resource, naming the principals that may use it. (Chapter 9)
Role / ClusterRole
Rules within a namespace / cluster-wide (or reusable). (Chapter 16)
Role explosion
Roles multiplying because they encode extra dimensions such as location. (Chapter 6)
Role session
A period of use of a role, with its own ARN and temporary credentials. (Chapter 8)
RoleBinding / ClusterRoleBinding
Grants of a role to subjects in a namespace / everywhere. (Chapter 16)
Root user
The account's original email-and-password identity, with unrestricted access. (Chapter 7)
Rotation
Issuing a new refresh token at each use, and treating reuse as theft. (Chapter 3)
Replacing a secret's value regularly, without downtime. (Chapter 18)

S

S3 Object Lock
Write-once storage that prevents deletion before a retention date. (Chapter 23)
Salt
A random per-password value hashed with it, so identical passwords give different hashes. (Chapter 2)
SCIM
A standard REST API for provisioning users and groups. (Chapter 13)
Scope
A named slice of access a client requests and a token carries. (Chapter 4)
SCP
Service control policy: an organisation ceiling on principals in member accounts. (Chapter 10)
Service control policy: a ceiling on principals' permissions in member accounts. (Chapter 20)
Secrets Manager
AWS's service for storing and rotating secrets. (Chapter 18)
Separation of duties
Splitting sensitive tasks so no one person can complete them alone. (Chapter 6)
Service account
A pod's identity for the Kubernetes API, and the anchor for its cloud role. (Chapter 16)
Service provider (SP)
The application that relies on the IdP's assertions. (Chapter 5)
Service role
A role an AWS service assumes to act for you. (Chapter 8)
Session
The state that lets a server recognise later requests after one authentication. (Chapter 3)
Session policy
A policy passed at session creation that narrows a role session. (Chapter 10)
Session theft
Stealing an authenticated session's cookie or token, skipping passwords and MFA. (Chapter 25)
SigV4
AWS Signature Version 4: HMAC signing of API requests with derived keys. (Chapter 19)
Source identity
An unchangeable value recorded for every action in a session and its chained sessions. (Chapter 8)
Source of truth
The system whose record decides; for people, usually HR. (Chapter 13)
SSRF
Server-side request forgery: making a server send requests on an attacker's behalf. (Chapter 15)
Standing access
Privilege held permanently, whether used or not. (Chapter 14)
Statement
One rule in a policy: effect, actions, resources and optional conditions. (Chapter 9)
STS
AWS Security Token Service, which issues temporary credentials. (Chapter 8)
sub claim
The token's subject; for GitHub, the repository plus branch, environment or pull request. (Chapter 17)

T

Tabletop exercise
Walking through an incident scenario on paper to find gaps. (Chapter 25)
Task role / execution role
An ECS task's role for its code, and the ECS agent's role for starting it. (Chapter 15)
TOTP
Time-based one-time password: an HMAC of the current 30-second step and a shared secret. (Chapter 2)
Trust policy
The resource-based policy on a role that says who may assume it. (Chapter 8)
Two-person rule
Requiring two people for an action, not just for its approval. (Chapter 14)

V

Vault lock
An AWS Backup setting that stops anyone deleting backups before their retention ends. (Chapter 21)

W

Watch list
The short set of events that raise alerts, each with a response. (Chapter 23)
Webhook
An HTTP callback a partner sends to report an event. (Chapter 19)
Workload identity
The identity software uses to call cloud APIs. (Chapter 15)
